newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Last HK colonial land auction sees mixed response.
newsitem.headline: Last HK colonial land auction sees mixed response.

text.p: Hong Kong launched its final land auction before Chinese rule to a muted audience on Tuesday, but sombre reserve finally turned into avid bidding, showing selective confidence in the property market, analysts said.
Hong Kong developers kept a stony silence for 15 minutes when auctioneer R.C. Baram asked HK$5.2 billion (US$672 million) for a 571,848 square foot plot in beachside Stanley.

After sluggish bidding the site on the southern side of Hong Kong island was finally sold to a consortium led by Paliburg Holdings Ltd for HK$5.5 billion, below analysts predictions of HK$6.4 billion to HK$7.3 billion.
There was more enthusiasm when the government opened bidding for a 79,675 square foot waterfront site in Hunghom on the Kowloon peninsula at HK$3.8 billion.
Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd and Hutchison Whampoa Ltd snapped up the site for HK$6.06 billion, well above expectations of HK$4 billion to HK$5 billion.
"The first site was like watching paint dry," said Michael Clarke, professional services director at Colliers Jardine. "Hunghom was spectacularly more successful."

Analysts said interest in the Stanley site was poor because the plot, likely to be used for low-rise luxury housing, was in a remote part of the island where prices were already high. It drew only four bidders.
"It is not an easy site," said Margaret Brooke, managing partner at Brooke Hillier Parker.
"Developers were sensible. They saw where the real value was rather than getting carried away with a difficult site."
Analysts said Hong Kong's plans to release more land for high-end housing development in 1997 and 1998 had also dampened interest.

"The Stanley site was not a very good price. It translates to around HK$13,000 per square foot," said Desmond Cheung, an analyst at Vickers Ballas. "The development cost is around HK$16,000 so you are looking at a selling price of HK$20,000, which is not that demanding."
Property was already selling around that price in the area, showing developers saw little upside, he said. "The current price is too expensive so developers are not that confident."
The Stanley sale sent property stocks into a tailspin, dragging Hong Kong's blue-chip Hang Seng Index down 1.54 percent to close at 14,760.17 points.
But analysts said investors were unable to react to the Hunghom sale, which concluded after the stock market closed.
"Bidding accelerated quite quickly after the market closed so I think property shares will rebound tomorrow," said Cheung.
The residential site drew bids from Swire Pacific Ltd, Sino Land Co Ltd and Lai Sun Development Co Ltd.
"There was a lot of bidding from a number of bidders, which is always a healthy sign," said Clarke. "It shows continuing confidence in the property market post July 1."
Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
Cheung said the Hunghom price translated into a "demanding" valuation of HK$8,500 per square foot. "To sell for a profit they have to demand a selling price of HK$13,000 to HK$14,000."
Cheung Kong is currently offering flats at a neighbouring project at around HK$10,000 per square foot, he said.
Franklin Lam, director of property research at SBC Warburg, said the Hong Kong developer had a vested interest in bidding up the price.
"Cheung Kong is selling Laguna Verde so they buy at a higher price now and sell at a higher price tomorrow," he said.
After Sino Land and Swire Pacific dropped out of the bidding, the breadth of bidders was quite narrow, he added.
"This auction shows reserve because of the lack of breadth and the low price for the first site," said Lam.
A third site -- a residential plot of 24,111 square feet on Lantau island -- sold for HK$40 million.
